paragraphs.text: 41.1 1 The acute response involves changes in every hormonal axis and is considered fully adaptive, helping the body to manage physio logic stress. Acute stress stimulates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, causes peripheral inactivation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) and hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axes, induces insulin resistance, and increases secre tion of growth hormone (GH), prolactin (PRL) and arginine vasopressin (AVP). Severity of illness has been associated with a greater degree of change of multiple hor monal axes (thyroid [2, 3], adrenal [4–6], sodium and AVP [7–12], and glucose [6, 13–16]), including studies that measure hor mone alteration at ICU admission. These hormonal alterations thus may have utility as endocrine vital signs, that is, markers of ill ness severity, and future prospective studies can consider if critical care interventions guided by hormone measurement at ICU admission might improve outcomes.

The chronic response, on the other hand, is characterized by central suppression of the HPT, HPG, and GH axes, as well as decreased production of PRL. These changes are associ ated with continued insulin resistance and a state of profound protein catabolism that is associated with significant morbidity and mor tality but has not, to date, been reversible. Whether this chronic response or its compo nents are adaptive remains uncertain. The advent of modern critical care has allowed humans to survive prolonged catastrophic ill ness that previously would have been univer sally fatal. From an evolutionary standpoint, it can be argued that the hormonal response to this unnatural scenario may not be adaptive, as any response would not have yielded a mean ingful survival advantage. In fact, a close exam ination of these hormonal responses to chronic critical illness demonstrates changes that may be considered quite maladaptive [1, 17].

The adrenocortical response is arguably the single most important hormonal response to critical illness: lacking it, patients may quickly succumb to their illness, as documented by Brown-Sequard in 1956 [18]. The initial adre nal response has traditionally been character ized by high serum ACTH and subsequent cortisol concentrations up to six times nor mal. As critical illness evolves, patients are at risk of developing critical illness-related corti costeroid insufficiency (CIRCI), a phenome non of insufficient glucocorticoid activity attributed to multiple changes in glucocorti coid homeostasis during critical illness: dys regulated hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, reduced clearance of plasma cor tisol, and tissue-resistance to cortisol. In CIRCI, the unbalanced systemic inflamma tion of critical illness is driven by overacti vated inflammatory pathways unchecked by an insufficient HPA axis response. Low or high basal levels of cortisol have been associ ated with poor outcomes, but these studies often have small sample sizes, risk of bias, and are inconsistently replicated [4, 6, 19].

paragraphs.text: Increased release of ACTH is driven by increased hypothalamic stimulation from
paragraphs.heading: 41.2 Adrenal Axis

paragraphs.text: corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) and AVP, contributing to a loss of the circadian rhythm of cortisol secretion [20]. There is variability in the ACTH-response to critical illness, as recent evidence has shown that ACTH levels are often only transiently increased or not increased at all [21, 22]. Acute elevations in cortisol concentrations may be driven in part by direct adrenal stimulation by cytokines, in addition to hypothalamicpituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis signaling, which is also upregulated in part via cytokine signal ing [20]. Increasingly, studies also show that cortisol concentrations may be elevated acutely not due to increased production but rather secondary to decreased breakdown due to altered expression and activity of hepatic and renal enzymes that metabolize cortisol, in addition to increased peripheral tissue activa tion of cortisone to cortisol [20, 23, 24], which has important diagnostic and treatment impli cations.
paragraphs.heading: 41.2 Adrenal Axis

paragraphs.text: Cortisol suppresses inducible nitric oxide synthetase (iNOS) and thereby substantially enhances vascular tone and increases blood pressure; iNOS is otherwise upregulated in sepsis with resultant hypotension. Cortisol also enhances the inotropic and vasopressor response to catecholamines and angiotensin
paragraphs.heading: 41.2 Adrenal Axis

paragraphs.text: II, which additionally support blood pressure. A high level of cortisol also induces profound insulin resistance, which accelerates glycoge nolysis and mobilizes precursors for gluco neogenesis by increasing protein catabolism and lipolysis. The result is a shunting of energy resources away from peripheral organs and toward the brain and heart. Cortisol also enhances free water clearance. Finally, corti sol suppresses elements of the immune sys tem, which may be important in preventing an over-exuberant, and potentially destructive, immune response [25].
paragraphs.heading: 41.2 Adrenal Axis

paragraphs.text: Once the patient enters the chronic phase of critical illness, ACTH levels remain low, and cortisol concentrations remain elevated. Potential mediators of these effects include atrial natriuretic peptide, substance P, and endothelin as well as the negative feedback on ACTH from nitric oxide and increased corti sol levels. ACTH suppression may therefore result in central adrenal insufficiency and thereby some extent of adrenal gland atrophy. Production of other adrenal steroids, includ ing mineralocorticoids and androgens, is rela tively suppressed during the chronic phase. This change appears to constitute an overall shift by the adrenal axis toward prioritizing hypercortisolism, whether by upregulating production or by downregulating cortisol metabolism.
paragraphs.heading: 41.2 Adrenal Axis

paragraphs.text: The potential disadvantages of this hor monal constellation include increased protein catabolism that leads to myopathy and impaired wound healing, as well as continued immune suppression at a time when the patient is increasingly susceptible to infectious complications. On the other hand, potential benefits may derive from positive hemody namic effects, both direct and indirect, medi ated through the adrenal medulla. In particular, epinephrine is produced via meth ylation of norepinephrine by phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), whose mRNA expression and enzy matic activity are induced by initial high intraadrenal concentrations of cortisol (esti mated at 50 times above circulating concen trations) and, independent of intraadrenal cortisol levels, by continued stress of critical illness [26–28].
paragraphs.heading: 41.2 Adrenal Axis

paragraphs.text: There are variable data on cortisol produc tion rates and corticosteroid resistance in crit ical illness, which in part correlates with severity of illness, but may also indicate differ ent subgroups of cortisol responses to illness. Studies of septic shock have shown a subset of patients with reduced cortisol synthesis, potentially due to inadequate stores of esteri fied cholesterol (the precursor to cortisol) and iatrogenic inhibition of the HPA axis and adrenal cortisol synthesis [20]. Tissue resis tance to cortisol can contribute to CIRCI, with multifactorial drivers of resistance including imbalanced signaling of glucocorti coid response elements that can activate or repress proinflammatory pathways; differen tial tissue expression of glucocorticoid core ceptor proteins; and differences in DNA methylation and chromatin structure [20].

The evaluation of suspected adrenal insuffi ciency is discussed in another chapter. Since absolute adrenal insufficiency is uncommon, generally the question in the critical care set ting is whether cortisol activity is sufficient for the severity of illness a patient is experiencing. Several clinical studies have implicated such “relative” adrenal insufficiency, i.e., CIRCI, as a risk factor for poor outcomes, primarily in the setting of septic shock [29, 30]. In this con text, the Society of Critical Care Medicine 2017 Guidelines state that CIRCI is impli cated if there is either failure of the serum cor tisol concentration to increase by more than 9 mcg/dL 1 h after stimulation with high-dose (250 mcg) ACTH or a random plasma corti sol of <10 mcg/dL, though the authors note that given the multifaceted nature of CIRCI, there is no evidence for a single test to reliably diagnose CIRCI [31]. Critically ill patients with baseline cortisol levels that are low (<10 mcg/dL) or very high (>34 mcg/dL) may also be at higher risk [29, 32, 33]. Adding to the complexity, while random cortisol levels may be sufficiently high to obviate the need for ACTH stimulation testing, a large retro spective analysis indicated that a low random cortisol does not necessarily indicate adrenal
paragraphs.heading: 41.2.1 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: dysfunction [34]. Specific diagnostic guide lines for critically-ill pediatric patients have recently been developed by the Pediatric Organ Dysfunction Information Update Mandate (PODIUM) Collaborative [6]. The PODIUM criteria defines adrenal axis dys function, following ACTH stimulation in patients with suspected primary adrenal insuf ficiency, as either peak serum cortisol concen tration < 18 mcg/dL or an increase in serum cortisol <9 mcg/dL. The PODIUM authors recommend measuring poststimulation corti sol levels either 30 min after a low-dose test of 1 mcg ACTH or 1 h after a high-dose test of 10 mcg/kg or maximum 250 mcg ACTH.
paragraphs.heading: 41.2.1 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Adult data are conflicting as to whether treat ment of CIRCI or empiric therapy in the criti cal care setting improves clinical outcomes, and pediatric data are scant. In the four larg est prospective RCTs in the last 20 years, the median age was 60–66 years, with underlying diagnoses of cancer, cardiovascular disease, stroke, and diabetes, all of which are factors arguing potently against using these data to guide care of critically ill children. Furthermore, in the largest recent survey of the literature, a 2019 Cochrane Review included 61 RCTs involving 12,192 patients only 533 of which were children, exemplifying the need for more data in pediatric critical ill ness [35].
paragraphs.heading: 41.2.2 Treatment

paragraphs.text: For critically ill adults, several small stud ies and meta-analyses have suggested a benefit to treatment of CIRCI. A large prospective, randomized, controlled trial (RCT) demon strated decreased mortality in adult patients with severe septic shock and CIRCI who were treated with hydrocortisone early in their clin ical course [36]. On the other hand, a larger RCT demonstrated no significant benefit of hydrocortisone in adult septic shock, even in patients with CIRCI [37]. Recent evidence from an RCT has also demonstrated no statis tically significant effect of hydrocortisone treatment on the development of shock among adults with severe sepsis, regardless of whether they had CIRCI or not [38]. Whether
paragraphs.heading: 41.2.2 Treatment

paragraphs.text: a true benefit exists, and in precisely which patients, remain uncertain. In a different clini cal setting, continuous hydrocortisone infu sion decreased ICU length of stay and the risk of hospital-acquired pneumonia in adult patients who were admitted to the ICU for multiple trauma and had CIRCI [39].
paragraphs.heading: 41.2.2 Treatment

paragraphs.text: In children with sepsis, as mentioned, pro spective RCTs are small and scarce. The con sequential data to the current debate were produced by the late Hector Wong and are retrospective in nature, so are compelling but not yet actionable. They suggest that there are distinct subpopulations of children with sep tic shock, identifiable by their mRNA and cytokine signatures, some of whom are harmed and others whom are helped by treat ment with hydrocortisone [40–42]. Thus, there may be a role for hydrocortisone therapy, but until large prospective RCTs can be completed (e.g. NCT03401398 currently underway) ther apeutic recommendations will remain vague, such as the 2020 Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines which recommend “+/− hydrocor tisone” with the caveat that “hydrocortisone may produce benefit or harm [43].”
paragraphs.heading: 41.2.2 Treatment

paragraphs.text: Notably, a currently controversial area of clinical use of hydrocortisone is in preterm and very low birth weight (VLBW) infants who frequently have hypotension after birth. It is known that cortisol levels increase as ges tation progresses, and VLBW infants are often found to have lower cortisol levels which may lead to decreased effectiveness of intrave nous catecholamines [44]. The latest Cochrane Review on this subject found only four studies with which to explore the use of hydrocorti sone either as a primary or secondary medica tion for hypotensive preterm infants, and the outcomes were equivocal. The authors con cluded that hydrocortisone may be as effective as dopamine for primary treatment of hypo tension in this group, but because long-term safety data are lacking, they do not routinely recommend its use [45].
paragraphs.heading: 41.2.2 Treatment

paragraphs.text: An important caveat that must be consid ered in the interpretation of any clinical trial involving the adrenal axis is the use of etomi date, even as a single-dose induction agent for intubation. It blocks synthesis of cortisol and will reliably suppress circulating cortisol con
paragraphs.heading: 41.2.2 Treatment

paragraphs.text: centrations for 24–48 h [46] although its use has not been consistently shown to lead to inferior clinical outcomes [47–49]. In light of these documented effects on cortisol produc tion, we recommend empiric administration of hydrocortisone at stress dosing (50 mg/m2/ day) for a discrete 48-h course after use of etomidate in patients with septic shock. Other commonly used medications in the intensive care setting have also been found to poten tially suppress plasma cortisol levels, includ ing opioids, propofol, and dexmedetomidine [50, 51].
paragraphs.heading: 41.2.2 Treatment

paragraphs.text: Assessing thyroid function in critically ill patients, as in healthy patients, can be extremely challenging. Ultimately, the clini cian would like to quantify the systemic actions of circulating thyroid hormones and then determine whether that level of activity is appropriate to the clinical scenario. As there is currently no direct measure of peripheral thy roid hormone functional activity, we generally depend on the patient’s serum thyroidstimulating hormone (TSH) concentration to provide an index of whether the brain is “sat isfied” with available concentrations of thy roxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). In the critically ill patient, however, this approach is no longer reliable, as the TSH level may remain normal despite a low serum level of T3, and possibly of T4 as well. This constella tion of thyroid function tests has been vari ously termed the “sick euthyroid syndrome,” “low T3 syndrome,” and hypothyroxinemia of “non-thyroidal illness” (NTI).
paragraphs.heading: 41.3 Thyroid Axis

paragraphs.text: 55 Under normal conditions, 35–40% of the T4 produced by the thyroid is eventually deio dinated to T3 in the liver and kidney, which accounts for almost all (80–90%) circulating T3 (the remainder is produced directly by the thyroid) [56]. As type I and II deiodinases are suppressed in the acute phase of illness, excess T4 is converted by type III deiodinase into biologically inactive reverse T3 (rT3), and cir culating T3 is likewise degraded to inert T2. Recent evidence also suggests that type III deiodinase itself is upregulated during critical illness, which may further decrease T3 and increase rT3 [57]. Multiple studies have asso ciated low T4, T3 and T3/rT3 ratios with poorer outcomes in critically ill neonates and children [3, 58]. In infants, the rise in rT3 is more pronounced than in older children [59]. Changes in TSH are less consistently associ ated with patient outcomes. The peripheral inactivation of thyroid hormones that char acterizes the acute phase of critical illness is likely adaptive for the patient in that it decreases overall metabolic rate in a period of physiologic stress, allowing available resources to be allocated to critical functions in the brain, heart, and immune system. Recent adult and pediatric RCTs have lent credence to this hypothesis in finding that delaying ini tiation of parenteral nutrition (PN) in criti cally ill patients, thereby restricting early macronutrient delivery, is associated with

fewer infections and faster recovery [58, 60, 61]. Subgroup analysis from recent adult and pediatric RCT found that delayed initiation of PN further reduced the T3-to-rT3 ratio, more pronounced in infants than older chil dren, which statistically explained part of the outcome benefit, indirectly providing evi dence of NTI’s adaptive role in acute critical illness [58, 62].

In the chronic phase of critical illness, TSH concentrations begin to decline into the lower third of the normal range despite low circulating T3 and, in some cases, low T4. Diminished TSH pulsatility and hypotha lamic thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) production correlate with low serum T3 [63, 64], which argues for a hypothalamic etiology of the euthyroid sick syndrome in the chronic phase of critical illness. This is supported by the ability of TRH infusion to reestablish nor mal TSH pulsatility and to increase T3 and T4 concentrations [65]. In prolonged critical ill ness, these changes in the thyroid axis may become maladaptive, as normal levels of T3 are required for protein synthesis, lipolysis, fuel utilization by muscle, and GH secretion and responsiveness. In the same pediatric RCT of delayed initiation of PN, decline in T4 levels was statistically correlated with a reduced outcome benefit of delayed PN, sug gesting that suppressed hypothalamicpituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis functioning may be a maladaptive response to critical illness [58], warranting more focused studies of this relationship.

Thyroid axis dysfunction in preterm neo nates is a distinct entity. Transient hypothy roxinemia of prematurity (THOP) has been observed in up to 50% of preterm and low birth weight (LBW) infants, with increased risk as gestational week decreases [66, 67]. Whereas the term “infants” have a character istic rise in thyroid hormone levels in the first week of life, some premature infants experi ence a transient period of low free T4, attenu ated T3 increase, and low or normal TSH levels that can persist through the first 6 weeks postnatally [2, 68]. In a retrospective cohort study of preterm newborns with or without THOP, multiple factors including anthropo

metrics, clinical diagnoses and medical treat ments were examined as possible associated factors, but only congenital heart disease, lower birth weight and small for gestational age status were associated with THOP [66]. THOP is complicated to distinguish from preterm infants with congenital hypothyroid ism, as preterm infants with congenital hypo thyroidism can present with a delayed TSH elevation [66, 69].

The etiology of THOP is likely multifac torial, including early withdrawal from the maternal supply of thyroid hormone, an immature hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis, altered peripheral thyroid hor mone metabolism, increased thyroid hor mone demand, altered iodine intake and metabolism, and/or HPT axis-altering medi cations. Preterm infants are at increased risk of iodine deficiency due to loss of maternal supply of iodine and low amounts of iodine in preterm formulas and parenteral nutrition. Iodine deficiency can contribute to slow infant recovery from THOP [70]. Another contributory factor is that these infants are often critically ill, thus for a subset of infants with THOP, non-thyroidal illness is likely contributing to the pattern of abnormal TFTs observed [2, 66, 67]. Non-thyroidal illness may present differently in infants, specifically, while low total T3 is observed frequently, the concomitant rise in reverse T3 is not consis tently observed [69].

The clinical effects of low serum T3 and T4 may be difficult to discern in the critically ill patient, and the indications for therapy are therefore difficult to define. Physiologic effects of a deficiency of thyroid hormones include elevated systemic vascular resistance (by up to 50%), decreased cardiac output, hyponatre mia, hypoglycemia, hypercholesterolemia, induction of a hypocoagulable state, hypo thermia, and decreased metabolic rate [71]. From a pulmonary standpoint, there is also a pronounced reduction in hypoxic and hyper capnic ventilatory drive [72] as well as com

paragraphs.text: promised skeletal muscle strength [73], diffusing capacity [74], and clearance of seda tion medications [75]. Though individual responses vary, these factors are rarely signifi cant enough to warrant thyroid hormone therapy for the changes of nonthyroidal ill ness alone, in the absence of true hypothyroid ism.
paragraphs.heading: 41.3.1 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Low total T3 is the most common labora tory abnormality in children with hypothyrox inemia of NTI. Free T3, however, when measured by equilibrium dialysis and radio immunoassay, was found to be normal in 21 of 25 (84%) adults with NTI [76]. Thus, the observed difference may be due more to alter ations in binding than to absolute drops in hormonal concentrations.
paragraphs.heading: 41.3.1 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Measurement of TSH should be per formed using a third-generation assay and
paragraphs.heading: 41.3.1 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: interpreted in the context of the patient’s overall clinical condition. During the acute phase of illness, TSH may be slightly elevated; during the chronic phase, it is usually normal or slightly low. TSH generally is also elevated during a period of clinical recovery, driving a resurgence of T4 output from the thyroid. The most reliable way to distinguish the etiology of an elevated TSH is to repeat the thyroid function tests 5–7 days later. If the abnormal ities are associated with clinical recovery, T4, T3, and TSH will each have migrated closer to the normal range, while in primary hypothy roidism the TSH will remain similarly or more elevated.

Measuring an index of TBG (e.g., TBGI, THBR, T3RU) is helpful in NTI. An elevated index, indicating a paucity of available TBGbinding sites, has been consistently associated with NTI and not hypothyroidism. As noted, in the critical care setting, we favor measure ment of total T3 and T4 along with an index of TBG over direct measurement of free T3 or free T4.

Reverse T3 measurement in NTI may be helpful early on in the course, as excess T4 is converted to rT3 rather than to T3. In princi ple, an elevated rT3 should distinguish NTI from true hypothyroidism, in which all thy roid hormones—including rT3—are expected to be low. After NTI has been established for several days, however, T4 production may be decreased; since less substrate is available for conversion to rT3, the serum concentration of rT3 may be misleadingly low. Furthermore, rT3 may be decreased in patients with renal failure and AIDS and occasionally elevated in patients with mild hypothyroidism. Therefore, rT3 cannot be used to reliably diagnose NTI [77].

As noted above, neonates represent a dis tinct subgroup when considering thyroid axis dysfunction. Hypothyroxinemia measured in premature infants can be transient and con sidered a normal phenomenon. As preterm infants grow and recover, TSH levels rise tran siently before returning to normal. However, a subgroup of infants go on to have persistent TSH elevation, and there are no current means to predict which infants will not spon taneously recover to normal TSH and thyroid

hormone levels [69]. Diagnostically, preterm infants, very LBW infants, and critically ill infants with true congenital, primary hypo thyroidism can have a delay in the TSH rise diagnostic of primary hypothyroidism [67, 69]. Thus, congenital hypothyroidism in these infants may be missed by initial newborn screening in the first few days of life. For this reason, recent consensus guidelines recom mend a second screen of thyroid function is recommended at 2 weeks postnatal or 2 weeks after the initial screen for the following groups: preterm neonates, LBW neonates (<1500 g), term or preterm neonates admitted to the NICU, neonates for whom the initial newborn screen was sent <24 h postnatal, or if possible false results from twin-twin transfusion [78]. Repeat TSH and free T4 measurements are also recommend for neonates with trisomy 21 (at 3–4 weeks of age) and infants with a family history of primary or central congenital hypo thyroidism [68]. NICU providers should refer to published gestation age and birth weight specific reference ranges when interpreting TFTs.

Another significant consideration prior to instituting therapy is concomitant medica tions [79]. Many of those commonly used in the ICU setting have profound effects on vari ous aspects of the HPT axis and are listed below. The impact of exogenous iodine can be especially detrimental in infants and patients with underlying thyroid dysfunction. In gen eral, iodine overload from excess exogenous iodine may lead to overproduction of thyroid hormone if left unchecked. The defense mech anism against this phenomenon is a downreg ulation of thyroid iodine update and incorporation into thyroid hormone, called the Wolff-Chaikoff effect. Infants, especially premature infants, are at increased risk of thy roid dysfunction in the setting of iodine expo sure. Premature infants have greater transdermal update of iodine due to increased skin permeability, and reduced renal clear ance of iodine. Iodine exposure is possible from multiple sources, including use of iodin ated disinfectants in the mother prenatally or during breastfeeding, or directly applied to the infant postnatally; iodinated contrast media; or iodine-containing medications.

Furthermore, immature thyroid gland func tion delays or prevents the reversal of the Wolff-Chaikoff effect after exogenous iodine exposure [69]. Multiple subsets of vulnerable patients are thought to be at risk to fail to adapt to the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, including neonates, patients with autoimmune thyroid disease or thyroiditis, history of thyroid sur gery, or use of certain medications including antithyroid drugs and lithium [80].

Iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (the Jod- Basedow phenomenon) can also occur with prolonged iodine exposure and may be tran sient or permanent, with risk factors including non-toxic or diffuse, nodular goiter or latent Graves’ disease [80]. Therefore, in infants or patients with underlying thyroid abnormali ties, iodine-induced hypothyroidism or hyper thyroidism is possible in the intensive care setting, where patients may receive multiple doses of iodine-containing contrast, iodinecontaining medications (amiodarone), or top ical iodine (with notable increased absorption in neonates and burn victims).

Direct supplementation with thyroid hor mone in the setting of NTI currently does not appear beneficial in non-cardiac adult patients, as demonstrated in prior RCTs [81, 82]. Studies of administration of T3 and/or T4 to critically ill adults inconsistently improved postoperative cardiac function in cardiac surgery patients, but otherwise has not been found to improve outcomes in differ ent ICU populations, and has been noted to suppress TSH which may delay HPT axis recovery [59]. It cannot, therefore, be recom mended as standard therapy for NTI in chil dren with non-cardiac critical illness. However, therapy may be justified if T3 is extremely low

paragraphs.text: and important clinical sequelae of hypothy roxinemia are apparent (e.g., severely elevated systemic vascular resistance, severe hypona tremia, or uncontrolled coagulopathy), although no data are currently available regarding this issue.

T3 has inotropic and chronotropic effects on the myocardium that may be beneficial, as demonstrated by clinical data obtained from T3 infusions in brain-dead organ donors [83]. This data has prompted several RCTs in post operative cardiac patients. In two adult trials, no benefit was demonstrated with an intrave nous loading dose of T3 followed by a T3 infusion [84, 85]. RCTs of T3 treatment in infants after cardiac surgery have shown mod est benefits including decreased time to nega tive fluid balance and reduced need for postoperative intensive care, but data on a direct improvement in cardiac function are conflicting [86–88]. The largest RCT to date in this population demonstrated no improve ment in time to extubation or cardiac function in patients treated with T3 postoperatively, although a benefit was seen in the youngest patients (<5 months) [89]. In a prospective study of Indonesian children age 3 years and younger undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass, oral T3 was given for 2.5 days post-operatively showed a reduced time to extubation, with the strongest degree of NTI and strongest effect of treatment noted in patients 5 months and younger, though there was no difference in the ICU or hospital length of stay, hemodynamic outcomes, or adverse events [90]. Thus, T3 treatment in children after cardiac surgery appears to have little risk and may have mod est benefits in very young infants. More pro spective data are needed before definitive recommendations may be made.
paragraphs.heading: Patients

paragraphs.text: Critically ill patients with known hypothy roidism should be continued on their out patient regimen of levothyroxine. Decompensation due to unrecognized hypo
paragraphs.heading: Thyroid Dysfunction

paragraphs.text: thyroidism or thyrotoxicosis in critically ill patients is rare in general and even more so in pediatrics, so the generalizability of practice recommendations from adult critical care should be considered carefully. Adult patients with longstanding but untreated hypothyroid ism can have myxedema coma triggered by cold exposure, vascular accidents, and infec tion. The features of myxedema coma include hypothermia and altered consciousness with elevated TSH and low levels of T4 and T3. Treatment includes replacing thyroid hor mone, treating the condition that triggered the patient’s decompensation, and providing stress dose hydrocortisone given the possibil ity of concomitant adrenal insufficiency [91]. Adult thyrotoxicosis in the setting of critical illness can present as suppressed TSH with elevated free T4 and normal T3 concentra tions (referred to as T4 thyrotoxicosis). Decompensated thyrotoxicosis, also known as thyroid storm, can be triggered by surgery or infection, and is characterized by CNS dys function, in addition to fever, supraventricu lar tachycardia, and GI distress. Management of thyroid storm includes antithyroid drugs, beta-blockers and intravenous glucocorti coids [91].
paragraphs.heading: Thyroid Dysfunction

paragraphs.text: Multiple retrospective cohort studies have associated THOP with adverse outcomes not explained by other recognized factors of mor bidity in preterm infants, though this is not a universal finding. While it has been demon strated that thyroid supplementation in healthy, term-infants with congenital hypo thyroidism benefits long-term neurodevelop mental outcomes, ideal management of THOP in premature and critically ill infants is unclear. Studies examining outcomes of infants with THOP treated with levothyroxine have mixed results, though the number of tri als investigating this question is small, and the doses and durations of treatment with levo thyroxine varied between studies [2]. One ran domized study of preterm infants <30 weeks gestation had no impact on neurodevelop mental outcomes at age 2 years, though
paragraphs.heading: of Prematurity

paragraphs.text: treated infants with a gestational age <27 weeks had significantly higher develop mental scores, whereas treated infants >27 weeks gestation had significantly lower developmental scores [92]. Another random ized study of levothyroxine supplementation until 32 weeks gestational age in infants born at <28 weeks gestation demonstrated improved neurodevelopmental outcomes at age 3 [93]. Treatment of suspected THOP in preterm neonates should be approached cau tiously, because there is some evidence in pre term infants that higher free T4 levels in the first 6 weeks of life is associated with poorer cognitive function, and several case reports describe circulatory dysfunction in preterm neonates treated with levothyroxine, thought to be related to an unmasking of relative adre nal insufficiency in prematurity [2]. Thus, it is possible that THOP is an adaptive response in at least a subset of neonates, overlapping with the likely benefit of NTI as described previ ously. Further studies are needed to inform the management of premature infants with THOP.
paragraphs.heading: of Prematurity

paragraphs.text: Levothyroxine (L-T4) is the mainstay of thy roid hormone replacement strategies, although in the setting of critical illness, it may cause rT3 to rise without any increase in T3 [82]. For patients with preexisting hypothy roidism not associated with NTI, T4 therapy should be continued at the usual dose while in the ICU. Due to incomplete absorption of T4 when administered orally, 75% of the enteral dose should be given intravenously to patients who cannot take the medication enterally [94, 95].
paragraphs.heading: and Dose

paragraphs.text: In the unique situation of severe hypothy roidism, a continuous intravenous infusion of T3 has the theoretical advantage of being titratable to the desired T3 concentration and effect. The risks of such an infusion include fatal arrhythmia in the case of overdosage, and that a prolonged infusion is expected to fully suppress TSH, creating an iatrogenic risk of myxedema coma upon cessation of ther apy. Therefore, general recommendations
paragraphs.heading: and Dose

paragraphs.text: even for the treatment of myxedema coma do not recommend therapy with T3 alone, but rather a combination of T3 and T4 [95, 96].
paragraphs.heading: and Dose

paragraphs.text: In the chronic phase of critical illness, con tinuous infusion of TRH has been demon strated to restore normal TSH pulsatility and increase T4 and T3 concentrations [65]. In principle, it is a safer option than direct thy roid hormone replacement, as the negative feedback of thyroid hormones on the pitu itary thyrotropes is maintained, thus preclud ing overstimulation of the thyroid axis. Multiple studies in critically ill adults of treat ment with different combinations of TRH, growth hormone releasing peptide 2, growth hormone releasing hormone and one with gonadotropin releasing hormone, did result in restoration of TSH pulsatility, improved lev els of pituitary hormones (GH, TSH, prolac tin), improved levels of thyroid hormone, sex steroids and downstream products of GH sig naling (when each of the upstream axes for those hormones were stimulated), as well as an improvement in markers of bone health and anabolism [91]. Further studies in adult patients and expansion to study in pediatric patients are needed to inform future treatment strategies.
paragraphs.heading: and Dose

paragraphs.text: The response of the GH axis to stress also fol lows a biphasic acute and chronic response to critical illness. In the acute phase, GH increases by a factor of three to five above baseline, initially associated with a rise in IGF-I. After several days of critical illness, baseline GH continues to be elevated, with pulsatile secretion at a frequency similar to that of healthy controls, but with a lower pulse amplitude. During the chronic phase, the GH/ IGF-I ratio may be elevated well above nor mal, consistent with what has been described as a state of GH insensitivity [97]. However, despite elevated baseline levels of GH, the integrated production of GH over time is decreased during chronic illness. In addition, IGF-I is known to be much more responsive to pulsatile GH production, which is altered in this state [98]. Furthermore, during the
paragraphs.heading: 41.4 Growth Hormone Axis

paragraphs.text: chronic phase (but not the acute phase), nor mal GH pulsatility and concentrations of IGF-I can be restored by continuous infusion of GH secretagogues [99]. These data suggest that the alterations in the GH axis during chronic critical illness are primarily central in origin, and not due to GH insensitivity.

Other important regulators of GH secre tion in the ICU setting include thyroid hor mone, glucocorticoids, and dopamine. In the setting of true hypothyroidism or hypothyrox inemia of non-thyroidal illness, GH has markedly decreased pulsatility. This is pre dominantly a pituitary effect, as thyroid hor mones are needed for GH gene transcription, translation, and secretion, although there are documented hypothalamic and peripheral effects as well [100, 101]. Glucocorticoids acutely stimulate GH secretion but beyond 12 h lead to a prolonged suppression of GH concentrations. Glucocorticoids also raise the serum concentration of IGF-I but inhibit its biological activity. Glucocorticoid deficiency, on the other hand, impairs the GH response to GHRH [102–105]. Dopamine infusions suppress GH production at the level of the pituitary, even at doses as low as 5 mcg/kg/ min. Rebound elevations in GH concentra tions occur within 20 min of discontinuation of dopamine, however, and persist for at least a day [106, 107].

The diagnosis of true GH insufficiency during critical illness is extremely difficult due to the dissociation of IGF-I levels from GH secre tion and to the lack of predictability of ran dom GH levels. Stimulation testing is often impractical, and may be uninformative, given that the individual is already stressed. Documentation of an elevated GH concentra tion, however, will reliably rule out GH insuf ficiency.
paragraphs.heading: 41.4.1 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: For patients with documented GH insuffi ciency, replacement of GH should be contin
paragraphs.heading: 41.4.2 Treatment

paragraphs.text: ued while in the ICU. Similarly, initiation of GH therapy is appropriate in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) when a new diag nosis of GH deficiency is made. The usual replacement dose for a neonate is 0.15–0.22 mg/kg/week divided into daily sub cutaneous doses. In any other clinical scenario involving critical illness, the use of GH is con traindicated, as the only large prospective, randomized, controlled trial demonstrated significantly increased mortality in adult ICU patients treated with GH [108]. This issue will be discussed further in the final section of this chapter.
paragraphs.heading: 41.4.2 Treatment

paragraphs.text: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism has been demonstrated in virtually all studies of sex hormones in critically ill adults. In adults responding acutely to a variety of severe stresses (e.g., sepsis, trauma, burns, starva tion), there is an initial surge in LH, while FSH and inhibin remain in the normal range, and testosterone and estradiol rapidly decrease [109, 110]. This short-term response of decreasing secretion of anabolic androgens may be adaptive as a means of decreasing energy consumption and allowing substrates to be utilized for other functions [3]. As the patient enters the chronic phase of critical ill ness, they become hypogonadotropic, and the low sex steroid levels persist [111, 112]. This likely represents the common pattern of peripheral hormonal suppression and pitu itary activation in the acute phase of illness, followed by hypothalamic-based pituitary and peripheral suppression in the chronic phase. In a small study of critically ill men, intravenous pulsatile infusion of GnRH only partially overcame their hypogonadotropic hypogonadism pointing toward the interac tions between the multiple endocrinologic axes disturbed during critical illness and their interdependence on one another [113].
paragraphs.heading: 41.5 Gonadal Axis

paragraphs.text: Recent studies of adults with COVID-19 have demonstrated an inverse correlation between total testosterone levels and both clinical and biochemical markers of illness severity [114–116]. Lower total testosterone
paragraphs.heading: 41.5 Gonadal Axis

paragraphs.text: was an independent risk factor for in-hospital mortality. Furthermore, higher estradiol to testosterone ratios were also associated with disease severity and mortality risk, which may be attributable to upregulation of aromatase activity in adipose tissue in critical illness [114–116]. One study of males critically ill with COVID-19 found significantly higher estradiol levels and lower testosterone levels than multiple age-matched control cohorts, including COVID-19 negative patients with coronary heart disease, COVID-19 negative ICU patients and healthy male blood donors [117]. Estradiol levels correlated with disease severity in males with a trend toward signifi cance in females, but this was not seen in other studies critical illness due to COVID-19 [117]. Therefore, testosterone levels are a demon strated biomarker of disease severity in adult males with COVID-19, while an association between sex hormones and COVID-19 illness severity has not been demonstrated in females, and studies in pediatric patients are lacking.
paragraphs.heading: 41.5 Gonadal Axis

paragraphs.text: In general, very little data exist for children with respect to gonadal axis changes during critical illness. In one recent prospective observational study, prepubertal children undergoing major cardiac surgery were found to have postoperative increases in several uri nary sex hormone metabolites, with the increases largest for estradiol and progester one [118]. Notably, however, these levels were 24-h collections pre- and post-surgery and therefore did not capture any changes in levels after the first 24 h postoperatively.
paragraphs.heading: 41.5 Gonadal Axis

paragraphs.text: Laboratory evaluation of hypogonadism should be approached skeptically in the set ting of critical illness. High or “inappropri ately normal” concentrations of gonadotropins may be encountered early in the clinical course and do not necessarily indi cate primary gonadal failure. Likewise, low gonadotropins are uninformative even in the acute phase, as they may be suppressed by elevated prolactin, dopamine infusion, or an early progression into the chronic phase of critical illness.
paragraphs.heading: 41.5.1 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Several sex hormone replacement trials have been attempted, largely in an attempt to treat the catabolic state of critical illness. These studies will be addressed in the final section of this chapter. For patients on sex hormone replacement therapy prior to critical illness, we recommend discontinuing it for the dura tion of the ICU stay, or until the child has begun to show signs of significant clinical recovery.
paragraphs.heading: 41.5.2 Treatment

paragraphs.text: AVP release is a known response to biological stress, triggered by hypovolemia, hyperosmo lality, hypotension, pain, and nausea, among many other physiologic stimuli. Multiple nuclei in the hypothalamus make AVP, which is then either transported to the posterior pituitary via axonal transport, or, released into the pituitary portal system and carried to the corticotrophs, where AVP likely synergizes with CRH to promote ACTH secretion from the anterior pituitary. Aberrant hyper- or hyposecretion of AVP is thought to occur in the setting of critical illness not of primary neurologic etiology, though further studies are needed to understand the underlying bio logic mechanisms. Neurologic trauma, CNS infection or injury, or neurosurgery can also lead to dysfunctional AVP secretion. In vaso dilatory shock, which is a predominant shock physiology in adults but uncommon in chil dren, a biphasic AVP pattern has been pro posed, in which an initial, acute increase in AVP gives way to AVP deficiency, possibly caused by depletion of AVP stores, impaired baroreceptor reflex, downregulated AVP syn thesis and/or downregulated AVP receptors [119]. It remains unclear if this possible state of AVP deficiency contributes to the patho physiology of critical illness in pediatric cohorts. The potential pathologic role of AVP in critical illness also requires further investi gation. In adult patients, some hypothesized that AVP may directly impact myocardial
paragraphs.heading: and Dysnatremia

paragraphs.text: contractile function, alter vascular tone of renal microvasculature and increase energy demands on different renal cell populations, and may therefore directly contribute to the development of kidney injury and disease.

Copeptin, cleaved from the AVP precursor molecule during vasopressin synthesis, has recently emerged as a valuable biochemical proxy for AVP given the increased circulating half-life and biochemical stability of copeptin relative to AVP. In a prospective, observa tional study of critically ill adults, copeptin was associated with disease severity scores, multiple biomarkers of critical illness, and mortality [9]. Multiple studies have demon strated that copeptin is a significant predictor of mortality in adults with acute and chronic heart failure and with acute myocardial infarc tion [10], as well as a predictor of complica tions and mortality in severe acute pancreatitis [120].

Copeptin has also been studied as a prog nostic marker in pediatric critical illness. In pediatric cardiac surgery and in children with acute heart failure, copeptin levels signifi cantly correlated with clinical outcomes including prognosis, inotropic score and ICU complications (in surgical patients) [121], and echocardiographic markers of decreased car diac function (in heart failure) [122]. Copeptin levels in a mixed cohort of pediatric ICU patients have been positively associated with length of stay, duration of mechanical ventila tion, primary ICU diagnosis, and vasopressor treatment intensity, though only vasopressortreatment intensity remained significant on a multivariate analysis [123]. Interestingly, there is some evidence that a subset of pediatric, cardiac postoperative patients may have rela tive AVP deficiency, defined as a lack of AVP rise above the reference range postoperatively, which may correlate with postoperative out comes and responsiveness to exogenous AVP [124], though this has been inconsistently demonstrated in pediatric cohorts [119, 123]. Future studies are needed to assess the prog nostic value of copeptin in the critically ill pediatric population, and to understand how copeptin levels may be used to guide clinical care. Additionally, there is mixed evidence for the prognostic utility of copeptin in pediatric
pneumonia [125, 126], and additional studies are needed to understand the clinical utility of copeptin levels in these and other cohorts of pediatric patients.

In neonates, elevated cord blood copeptin levels have been correlated with acute birth asphyxia, intraventricular hemorrhage, meco nium stained amniotic fluid and neonatal dis tress regardless of delivery route [127–129] though this has not been consistently demon strated [130]. One challenge is that cord blood copeptin levels are substantially elevated in healthy term and preterm infants following vaginal birth compared to routine caesarean birth [131–133]. Nonetheless, cord blood copeptin has been significantly, negatively correlated with umbilical artery pH and base excess even in neonates born via vaginal deliv ery [127–129, 132, 133]. Among infants born via caesarean delivery only, elevated copeptin levels have been associated with abnormal fetal heart tracings, reduced placental perfu sion, and early onset sepsis [131]. In a study of IUGR neonates following caesarean birth, cord blood copeptin levels were significantly higher in those with IUGR compared to agematched AGA controls, and positively corre lated with prenatal umbilical artery resistance in IUGR fetuses [134], though another study showed no difference when controlling for delivery mode [135]. Future studies will pro vide further insight into the prognostic utility of cord blood copeptin levels and how this marker can be incorporated into clinical prac tice to improve neonatal outcomes.

Dysnatremia, encompassing hyponatre mia (serum sodium <135 mmol/L) and/or hypernatremia (serum sodium >145 mmol/L) has been associated with worse outcomes in critically ill infants and children. The contri butions of AVP to dysnatremia in critical ill ness requires further investigation. Generally speaking, there is a known risk of hospital acquired hyponatremia in children, which is twice as high in children with a primary car diac diagnosis [8]. Both adult and pediatric studies have shown that hyponatremia is an independent risk factor for mortality and increased duration of hospital stay [11]. In a retrospective study of children hospitalized for heart failure, hyponatremia (serum sodium

<135 mmol/L) either identified on admission or developed during hospitalization, was independently associated with increased severity of critical illness (inotropic support and/or mechanical ventilation) and adverse outcomes (heart transplant, mechanical circu latory support, or death) [8]. It is unclear if there is any direct contribution of hyponatre mia to adverse outcomes or if the hyponatremia is only a marker of illness severity.

Hypernatremia is also associated with neg ative outcomes in infants with heart disease. A retrospective study of infants (<1 year old) following cardiac surgery demonstrated dys natremia in half of subjects, presenting sooner after surgery in infants younger than 30 days old and a sooner presentation of hypernatre mia versus hyponatremia (median onset of 5.8 h vs. 43.8 h). Hypernatremia was associ ated with longer length of stay and ventilation time, but not mortality, whereas none of these outcomes were associated with hyponatremia. Clinical characteristics associated with hyper natremia included younger age, higher surgi cal complexity, administration of bicarbonate and use of vasopressin, but not diuretic type or timing [7].

There is a high incidence of dysnatremia in NICU populations, which may be attributed in part to sodium concentrations in IV fluids and blood products [11]. In a large, multina tional study of dysnatremia and AKI in NICU patients during postnatal days 2–7, patients without AKI were noted to have an increased risk of mortality associated with hypernatremia (fourfold increase) or mixed hyponatremia and hypernatremia (7.5-fold increase). The group with mixed dysnatremia had the highest acuity of critical illness and the greatest sodium shifts, and an increased mortality rate regardless of the direction of the sodium shift [11]. The association between sodium levels and mortality was not observed in neonates with both AKI and dysnatremia. Hyponatremia occurred most commonly in neonates with a gestational age greater than or equal to 36 weeks, possibly due to the higher incidence of perinatal asphyxia in this population, driven by increased ADH secre tion or fluid resuscitation strategies in this population. Hypernatremia by comparison

occurred in a disproportionate number of neonates less than 29 weeks gestational age, and also noted to be associated with intraven tricular hemorrhage. Hypernatremia was seemingly not only attributable to excess insensible losses due to less than expected weight loss, and therefore may have also been promoted by sodium concentration in fluids delivered [11].

Studies in older children and adults have shown an association between dysnatremia, subsequent AKI, and other poor outcomes. A retrospective study of 5000 children demon strated that hyponatremia at ICU admission was associated with a 1.75 adjusted odds ratio for developing severe AKI, and a persistent association noted when adjusting for underly ing illness and comorbidities. The presence of hyponatremia multiplied the effect of AKI on risk of need for renal replacement therapy and hospital mortality [12]. Hyponatremia has been independently associated with mor tality in hospitalized pediatric and adult cohorts [12], though it is unclear if hyponatre mia plays a causal role in the subsequent development of AKI (possibly through direct cellular toxicity), or if the hyponatremia is a marker of either degree of illness, comorbid condition(s) leading to AKI, or a marker of early kidney injury itself. Overall, while there are many surgical and pharmacologic factors that can contribute to dysnatremia in the postoperative phase and in critical illness more broadly, an abnormal sodium level can be viewed as an indicator of more severe criti cal illness that requires careful assessment by the medical team. Future studies may help discern if dysnatremia plays a causative role in adverse outcomes.

The diagnosis and management of hyperna tremia is discussed in another chapter. In the setting of euvolemic or hypervolemic hypona tremia, more traditional therapies include fluid restriction, oral urea, hypertonic saline, lithium, demeclocycline. Oral urea has been used in patients with chronic SIADH and has also been studied in patients with new diagno
paragraphs.heading: 41.6.1 Diagnosis and Treatment

paragraphs.text: ses of SIADH in the ICU setting. Treatment with 45 g urea per day led to mean sodium lev els increasing by 7 mEq/L in the first 48 h and normalizing by the fourth day of urea therapy [136]. In a metaanalysis of critically ill pediat ric patients (postoperative patients and septic patients with meningitis), fluid restriction to between 1/2 and 2/3 of maintenance was asso ciated with a higher plasma sodium level, manifesting as improvement in hyponatremia or mitigation of decreasing plasma sodium levels. The European Society of Pediatric and Neonatal Intensive Care (ESPNIC) recom mended, in acute and critically ill children, avoiding fluid overload and cumulative posi tive fluid balance. ESPNIC recommends, in those at risk of increased endogenous ADH secretion, restricting maintenance fluids to 65–80% of maintenance, and in those at greater risk of edematous states (heart/renal/ hepatic failure), restricting to 50–60% of maintenance, though the strength of the evi dence was limited [137].

Vaptans have emerged as a therapeutic option for euvolemic and hypervolemic hypo natremia. Vaptans are type 2 vasopressin receptor antagonists that function in the renal collecting duct to promote free water excre tion, and are available as oral (tolvaptan) and intravenous (conivaptan) formulations. Tolvaptan has been studied more extensively in adult patients with heart failure [138], cir rhosis [138], and kidney disease [10]. In a study of tolvaptan in adults primarily as out patients with congestive heart failure, cirrho sis or SIADH, tolvaptan enabled the correction of mild and marked hyponatremia with only 4 of 223 patients (1.7%) overcor recting at a rate faster than 0.5 mmol per liter per hour [138]. In two studies of neurocriti cally ill adult patients with hyponatremia, tolvaptan increased serum sodium levels in all patients, with over-correction only occurring in patients who received 15 mg instead of 7.5 mg dose and risk factors for osmotic demyelinating syndrome (ODS), or patients who received two 15 mg doses of tolvaptan within 31 h of their first dose, with no reported symptoms of ODS [139, 140]. Interestingly, in a retrospective cohort study of adult patients with SIADH or CHF treated with tolvaptan

15 mg daily, a more rapid increase in serum sodium and higher incidence of overcorrec tion was noted in the SIADH vs CHF group. The differential response to tolvaptan in these two groups may be related to the underlying etiology of hyponatremia, including differ ences in intravascular volume, delivery of water to the collecting duct, and differences in renal function [141].

The use of vaptans in pediatric practice is relatively new but has shown promising effects. A 2022 systematic review compiled informa tion from case reports and case series describ ing the use of vaptans in pediatric patients with edematous or hyponatremic conditions, in which 85% of patients had congenital heart disease, but patients with kidney, oncologic and nervous system disease were also included [142]. Vaptans resulted in a significant increase in urine output in the edematous and the hyponatremic groups, with an increase in serum sodium in only the hyponatremic group with correction of serum sodium greater than 16 mmol/L in 48 h in only 5 of 22 cases with this information available [142]. The authors also reported two retrospective studies of oral tolvaptan in infants following cardiac surgery, including a study of capillary leak syndrome. Patients classified as tolvaptan responders had a significant increase in diuresis, reduc tion of body weight, correction of hyponatre mia, a reduction of the need for additional intravenous furosemide [143, 144], as well as earlier ability to wean ventilatory support [145]. The first prospective study of tolvaptan in pediatrics was conducted in children with nephrotic syndrome and furosemide-resistant, severe edema, and demonstrated a significant increase in urine volume and decrease in body weight when transitioned to combination therapy (oral tolvaptan and IV furosemide) compared to initial urine output in those patients receiving IV furosemide alone [146]. The study was small with 24 participants and no control group, and showed no significant change kidney function or complications of hypotension or hypovolemia, but two partici pants did develop asymptomatic hypernatre mia. Further prospective studies in pediatric cohorts are needed to understand the safety and efficacy of vaptans in pediatric cohorts,
especially given the potential for osmotic demyelination syndrome which has not been prospectively assessed in pediatric patients.

Critically ill infants and children are under severe catabolic stress. Protein loss is the hall mark of the metabolic stress response, and its extent is determined by the severity of illness [147, 148]. If protein loss persists, it is associ ated with increased morbidity and mortality [149]. Limiting protein degradation and maxi mizing protein accretion are of particular importance in children because of their lim ited protein reserves and their requirement for growth and development. Infants on extracor poreal life support (ECLS, also known as ECMO) are among the most profoundly ill children in pediatric critical care and quanti tatively demonstrate extremely high rates of protein loss [150]. Children who have suffered severe burns have also been studied exten sively in this regard and have been shown to remain catabolic for at least 1 year after their injury [151].
paragraphs.heading: Hormonal Interventions to Treat the Protein Catabolism of Critical Illness

paragraphs.text: The hormonal changes detailed earlier in the chapter—in particular, suppressed GH, elevated cortisol, and insulin resistance—con tribute to the catabolism of critical illness. They induce a milieu of protein catabolism, carbohydrate intolerance, and paradoxical fat sparing. Stress hyperglycemia may also directly impair tolerance of enteral nutrition and exacerbate protein catabolism [152]. A number of anabolic hormonal therapies, including GH, IGF-I, insulin, and androgens, have been administered in the past in an effort to counteract these maladaptive changes.
paragraphs.heading: Hormonal Interventions to Treat the Protein Catabolism of Critical Illness

paragraphs.text: GH (in the form of human pituitary extracts) was first used in an animal model of traumatic injury in 1941 to improve nitrogen retention and reduce weight loss [153]. Recombinant GH has since been investigated in a number of small clinical trials over a period of approximately 25 years. Small RCTs
paragraphs.heading: Hormonal Interventions to Treat the Protein Catabolism of Critical Illness

paragraphs.text: in a variety of ICU adult patients, using a variety of GH doses, documented improve ments in indices of protein turnover and clini cal outcome [154–157]. One moderate-sized pediatric study (N = 72) demonstrated decreased protein catabolism in burned chil dren treated from ICU discharge until 1 year from burn [158]. The adult studies prompted a large multicenter RCT in adults admitted to the ICU for 5–7 days. In this trial, which used a daily dose of 0.1 mg/kg, the relative risk of mortality in patients receiving GH was increased to 1.9–2.4 compared to those receiv ing placebo [108]. No clear rationale for the increased mortality has yet been demon strated, although hyperglycemia and associ ated immune compromise are suspected mediators. The FDA has since warned against the use of GH in patients with acute critical illness, and all related clinical trials outside of the burn population have effectively ceased [159].
paragraphs.heading: Hormonal Interventions to Treat the Protein Catabolism of Critical Illness

paragraphs.text: Other attempts to augment the suppressed somatotroph axis have focused on delivering IGF-I, with or without GH. In normal adult subjects, IGF-I therapy has multiple effects that are potentially desirable in critically ill patients, including (a) increasing glucose uptake three-fold; (b) reducing hepatic glu cose output by 60–70%; (c) lowering blood glucose acutely (IV, not SQ); (d) lowering insulin, c-peptide, glucagon, free fatty acids, and ketones; and (e) decreasing proteolysis and thereby decreasing plasma amino acid concentrations [160]. These effects persist in the fed state, with glucocorticoid-induced catabolism [161], and were confirmed in a nonrandomized fashion in stable, post-burn adults [162]. Unfortunately, three RCTs failed to demonstrate a significant effect in ill post operative adult patients [163–165]. In stable postburn children, one RCT demonstrated significant effects in mitigating the extent of protein catabolism using IGF-I in combina tion with IGF-BP3 [166]. IGF-I has also been shown to be safe in a Phase I clinical trial in critically ill adults [167].
paragraphs.heading: Hormonal Interventions to Treat the Protein Catabolism of Critical Illness

paragraphs.text: Anabolic sex steroid therapy in the criti cally ill with burns or trauma has produced several reports of positive results in adults [168–170] and one in burned children [158].

Oxandrolone, a nonaromatizable androgen, has been the therapeutic agent of choice due its decreased virilizing potency and hepato toxicity as compared to testosterone. Data from pediatric burn patients have demon strated a doubling of the fractional synthetic rate of protein and a substantial improvement in net protein balance [158]. An RCT in adult burn patients showed decreased length of stay in those treated with oxandrolone compared to placebo [171]. This finding was replicated in a large pediatric RCT that evaluated oxan drolone treatment in the acute phase of post burn care. This trial demonstrated that oxandrolone decreased length of stay, reversed loss of weight and lean body mass, and mark edly improved muscle strength several months after discharge [172]. Furthermore, a singlecenter RCT evaluated 5-year outcomes of safety and efficacy of oxandrolone use in severely burned pediatric patients and found improved long-term outcomes in height, bone mineral content, cardiac work, and muscle strength in the oxandrolone-treated group [173]. Although these data strongly support the utility of oxandrolone following burn injuries, whether it has a similar role in ame liorating the hypercatabolic state of other critical illnesses remains to be seen.

Insulin therapy has been studied in a wide variety of clinical situations in order to reduce protein breakdown and to stimulate protein synthesis and growth. In small numbers of healthy volunteers, insulin has suppressed proteolysis by 59–91%, in a dose-dependent manner [174–177]. In burned adults, protein synthesis was stimulated, and wound healing was accelerated [178–181]. Pediatric burn patients who received intensive insulin ther apy in a RCT had significant improvements in bone density, body fat, and lean body mass, as well as reduced markers of fat metabolism [182]. A study of four stable, premature neo nates demonstrated an 80% suppression of proteolysis but noted a significant rise in plasma lactate during the insulin infusion [181]. Another small (n = 12) randomized, prospective crossover trial of parenterally fed critically ill neonates on extracorporeal life support also demonstrated that insulin did indeed decrease proteolysis, but this study uti

lized supraphysiologic doses of insulin and only improved net protein balance in those who received adequate dietary protein [183]. However, in a larger RCT (n = 561) of young children age 0–36 months following cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, no degree of insulin therapy was found to miti gate skeletal muscle breakdown [184].

Aside from its potential broader role in preventing hypercatabolism, use of insulin infusions in critical care has been very actively investigated as a means of addressing the hyperglycemia that is common in critically ill patients. A great deal of evidence links uncon trolled hyperglycemia in critically ill adults and children with a variety of adverse out comes including morbidity, increased length of stay, and death [6, 13–16]. The PODIUM collaborative defines hyperglycemia in criti cally ill children as blood glucose >150 mg/dL [6]. Two large RCTs demonstrated that tight glucose control using an intravenous insulin infusion significantly reduced mortality by 29% in adult diabetics after myocardial infarc tion and by 34% in adult postoperative surgi cal ICU patients [185, 186]. Although these early findings were promising, subsequent tri als and meta-analyses of intensive glycemic control in critically ill adults have produced inconsistent results and have not shown a con vincing mortality benefit [187–192], with improbable benefit in traumatic brain injury patients [193]. Furthermore, the most recent large RCT demonstrated increased mortality in adults treated with intensive insulin man agement to near-normoglycemia, compared to those managed less aggressively [194].

Pediatric RCTs of intensive glycemic con trol in the ICU have largely found there to be no benefit to hospital mortality or rates of sepsis, with no significant difference in these outcomes found in a recent meta-analysis of six pediatric RCTs [195]. However, the trials that reported on the need for dialysis demon strated an association between intensive glyce mic control and a decrease in dialysis needs. In severely burned pediatric patients, a ran domized control trial demonstrated that intensive glycemic control improved morbid ity, including reduction in infection and sep sis, reduced postburn hepatomegaly, improved

metabolic measures, and reduced inflamma tory and acute-phase reactants [182]. In a small RCT of neonates undergoing congenital heart surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, intensive glycemic control significantly low ered hemodynamic support requirements and lactate levels, as well as markers of cardiac and systemic inflammation [196]. However, intensive glycemic control in pediatric critical illness has been uniformly associated with severe hypoglycemia [195, 197–199]. Overall, the current evidence does not support inten sive glycemic control in critically ill children, though there may be benefit in specific patient groups such as burn patients and neonates with congenital heart disease, that require fur ther investigation.

In contrast to the uncertainty regarding its possible benefits, evidence is unequivocal that intensive glycemic control carries an increased risk of hypoglycemia though the use of con tinuous glucose monitoring and advanced insulin dosing protocols can reduce, but not eliminate, this risk [200]. The PODIUM col laborative defines hypoglycemia in critically ill children as blood glucose <50 mg/dL [6]. Hypoglycemia in the intensive care setting is associated with complications of seizure, brain damage, and death in both adults and children [201, 202]. Therefore, the conflicting data from trials of intensive glycemic control may partly derive from increasing risks related to hypoglycemia in trials that treated to lower blood glucose targets. In summary, although uncontrolled hyperglycemia in critical illness is clearly associated with worse outcome, attempting to control blood glucose too tightly with insulin infusion does not defini tively improve outcomes and carries the risk of hypoglycemia. Therefore, current consen sus guidelines recommend an intermediate blood glucose target range of 140–180 mg/dL [13]. Further studies are necessary to assess the true benefits, risks, and appropriate degree of intensive glycemic control in critically ill children, and they are currently underway in the US and Europe. During the chronic phase of critical illness, the hypothalamus is sup pressed despite normal responsiveness of the remainder of the components of each hor monal axis. This is a state that, but for modern

critical care, human beings would not have survived to reach and have not evolved to endure. With this in mind, a final approach to hormonal therapies in critical illness is replacement of hypothalamic peptides by continuous (or pulsatile) infusion, which would be expected to reactivate normal pulsa tile production of pituitary hormones. The primary advantage of this approach is that it maintains negative feedback on the pituitary and should theoretically prevent overproduc tion of end hormones, each of which has its own maladaptive effects at excessive concen trations. For example, although GH itself has been deemed unsafe for use in this popula tion, infusion of GH secretagogues (e.g., GHRH, ghrelin) has been shown to normal ize GH and IGF-I concentrations in a physi ologic, pulsatile manner [203]. Co-administration of GH secretagogues, TRH, and pulsatile GnRH during the chronic state of critical illness has been shown to improve the function of all three axes simulta neously [91, 204]. However, further research investigating clinical outcomes using infu sions of hypothalamic peptides is required to definitively address this issue.

Key Points

5 There are two distinct endocrinologic

responses to critical illness: acute and chronic. The acute response is fully adaptive to physiologic stress, whereas the chronic response leads to prolonged insulin resistance and severe protein catabolism associated with significant morbidity and mortality. 5 Operational definitions and treatment

guidelines for critical illness-related cor ticosteroid insufficiency (or “relative” adrenal insufficiency) in children are lacking. ACTH stimulation testing con tinues to be guided by adult data, and future pediatric RCTs are needed. 5 “Sick euthyroid syndrome,” “low T3

syndrome,” and hypothyroxinemia of “non-thyroidal illness” (NTI) are syn onymous. Low total T3 is the most common laboratory abnormality in children with hypothyroxinemia of NTI. 5 Uncontrolled hyperglycemia in critical

illness is associated with worse out comes. However, attempting to control blood glucose too tightly with insulin infusion has not been shown to improve outcomes and carries the risk of hypo glycemia. Therefore, current consensus guidelines recommend an intermediate blood glucose target range of 140–180 mg/dL.

### 41.1 Paradigm of Endocrine

### Response to Acute Versus Chronic Critical Illness

### 41



41.1 1 The acute response involves changes in every hormonal axis and is considered fully adaptive, helping the body to manage physio logic stress. Acute stress stimulates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, causes peripheral inactivation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) and hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axes, induces insulin resistance, and increases secre tion of growth hormone (GH), prolactin (PRL) and arginine vasopressin (AVP). Severity of illness has been associated with a greater degree of change of multiple hor monal axes (thyroid [2, 3], adrenal [4–6], sodium and AVP [7–12], and glucose [6, 13–16]), including studies that measure hor mone alteration at ICU admission. These hormonal alterations thus may have utility as endocrine vital signs, that is, markers of ill ness severity, and future prospective studies can consider if critical care interventions guided by hormone measurement at ICU admission might improve outcomes.

The chronic response, on the other hand, is characterized by central suppression of the HPT, HPG, and GH axes, as well as decreased production of PRL. These changes are associ ated with continued insulin resistance and a state of profound protein catabolism that is associated with significant morbidity and mor tality but has not, to date, been reversible. Whether this chronic response or its compo nents are adaptive remains uncertain. The advent of modern critical care has allowed humans to survive prolonged catastrophic ill ness that previously would have been univer sally fatal. From an evolutionary standpoint, it can be argued that the hormonal response to this unnatural scenario may not be adaptive, as any response would not have yielded a mean ingful survival advantage. In fact, a close exam ination of these hormonal responses to chronic critical illness demonstrates changes that may be considered quite maladaptive [1, 17].


## PDF page 1065 | printed page 1071



### 41.2 Adrenal Axis

The adrenocortical response is arguably the single most important hormonal response to critical illness: lacking it, patients may quickly succumb to their illness, as documented by Brown-Sequard in 1956 [18]. The initial adre nal response has traditionally been character ized by high serum ACTH and subsequent cortisol concentrations up to six times nor mal. As critical illness evolves, patients are at risk of developing critical illness-related corti costeroid insufficiency (CIRCI), a phenome non of insufficient glucocorticoid activity attributed to multiple changes in glucocorti coid homeostasis during critical illness: dys regulated hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, reduced clearance of plasma cor tisol, and tissue-resistance to cortisol. In CIRCI, the unbalanced systemic inflamma tion of critical illness is driven by overacti vated inflammatory pathways unchecked by an insufficient HPA axis response. Low or high basal levels of cortisol have been associ ated with poor outcomes, but these studies often have small sample sizes, risk of bias, and are inconsistently replicated [4, 6, 19].

Increased release of ACTH is driven by increased hypothalamic stimulation from



1

corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) and AVP, contributing to a loss of the circadian rhythm of cortisol secretion [20]. There is variability in the ACTH-response to critical illness, as recent evidence has shown that ACTH levels are often only transiently increased or not increased at all [21, 22]. Acute elevations in cortisol concentrations may be driven in part by direct adrenal stimulation by cytokines, in addition to hypothalamicpituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis signaling, which is also upregulated in part via cytokine signal ing [20]. Increasingly, studies also show that cortisol concentrations may be elevated acutely not due to increased production but rather secondary to decreased breakdown due to altered expression and activity of hepatic and renal enzymes that metabolize cortisol, in addition to increased peripheral tissue activa tion of cortisone to cortisol [20, 23, 24], which has important diagnostic and treatment impli cations.

Cortisol suppresses inducible nitric oxide synthetase (iNOS) and thereby substantially enhances vascular tone and increases blood pressure; iNOS is otherwise upregulated in sepsis with resultant hypotension. Cortisol also enhances the inotropic and vasopressor response to catecholamines and angiotensin
