II, which additionally support blood pressure. A high level of cortisol also induces profound insulin resistance, which accelerates glycoge nolysis and mobilizes precursors for gluco neogenesis by increasing protein catabolism and lipolysis. The result is a shunting of energy resources away from peripheral organs and toward the brain and heart. Cortisol also enhances free water clearance. Finally, corti sol suppresses elements of the immune sys tem, which may be important in preventing an over-exuberant, and potentially destructive, immune response [25].

Once the patient enters the chronic phase of critical illness, ACTH levels remain low, and cortisol concentrations remain elevated. Potential mediators of these effects include atrial natriuretic peptide, substance P, and endothelin as well as the negative feedback on ACTH from nitric oxide and increased corti sol levels. ACTH suppression may therefore result in central adrenal insufficiency and thereby some extent of adrenal gland atrophy. Production of other adrenal steroids, includ ing mineralocorticoids and androgens, is rela tively suppressed during the chronic phase. This change appears to constitute an overall shift by the adrenal axis toward prioritizing hypercortisolism, whether by upregulating production or by downregulating cortisol metabolism.

The potential disadvantages of this hor monal constellation include increased protein catabolism that leads to myopathy and impaired wound healing, as well as continued immune suppression at a time when the patient is increasingly susceptible to infectious complications. On the other hand, potential benefits may derive from positive hemody namic effects, both direct and indirect, medi ated through the adrenal medulla. In particular, epinephrine is produced via meth ylation of norepinephrine by phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), whose mRNA expression and enzy matic activity are induced by initial high intraadrenal concentrations of cortisol (esti mated at 50 times above circulating concen trations) and, independent of intraadrenal cortisol levels, by continued stress of critical illness [26–28].

### 41

There are variable data on cortisol produc tion rates and corticosteroid resistance in crit ical illness, which in part correlates with severity of illness, but may also indicate differ ent subgroups of cortisol responses to illness. Studies of septic shock have shown a subset of patients with reduced cortisol synthesis, potentially due to inadequate stores of esteri fied cholesterol (the precursor to cortisol) and iatrogenic inhibition of the HPA axis and adrenal cortisol synthesis [20]. Tissue resis tance to cortisol can contribute to CIRCI, with multifactorial drivers of resistance including imbalanced signaling of glucocorti coid response elements that can activate or repress proinflammatory pathways; differen tial tissue expression of glucocorticoid core ceptor proteins; and differences in DNA methylation and chromatin structure [20].

### 41.2.1 Diagnosis

The evaluation of suspected adrenal insuffi ciency is discussed in another chapter. Since absolute adrenal insufficiency is uncommon, generally the question in the critical care set ting is whether cortisol activity is sufficient for the severity of illness a patient is experiencing. Several clinical studies have implicated such “relative” adrenal insufficiency, i.e., CIRCI, as a risk factor for poor outcomes, primarily in the setting of septic shock [29, 30]. In this con text, the Society of Critical Care Medicine 2017 Guidelines state that CIRCI is impli cated if there is either failure of the serum cor tisol concentration to increase by more than 9 mcg/dL 1 h after stimulation with high-dose (250 mcg) ACTH or a random plasma corti sol of <10 mcg/dL, though the authors note that given the multifaceted nature of CIRCI, there is no evidence for a single test to reliably diagnose CIRCI [31]. Critically ill patients with baseline cortisol levels that are low (<10 mcg/dL) or very high (>34 mcg/dL) may also be at higher risk [29, 32, 33]. Adding to the complexity, while random cortisol levels may be sufficiently high to obviate the need for ACTH stimulation testing, a large retro spective analysis indicated that a low random cortisol does not necessarily indicate adrenal


## PDF page 1067 | printed page 1073

dysfunction [34]. Specific diagnostic guide lines for critically-ill pediatric patients have recently been developed by the Pediatric Organ Dysfunction Information Update Mandate (PODIUM) Collaborative [6]. The PODIUM criteria defines adrenal axis dys function, following ACTH stimulation in patients with suspected primary adrenal insuf ficiency, as either peak serum cortisol concen tration < 18 mcg/dL or an increase in serum cortisol <9 mcg/dL. The PODIUM authors recommend measuring poststimulation corti sol levels either 30 min after a low-dose test of 1 mcg ACTH or 1 h after a high-dose test of 10 mcg/kg or maximum 250 mcg ACTH.

### 41.2.2 Treatment

Adult data are conflicting as to whether treat ment of CIRCI or empiric therapy in the criti cal care setting improves clinical outcomes, and pediatric data are scant. In the four larg est prospective RCTs in the last 20 years, the median age was 60–66 years, with underlying diagnoses of cancer, cardiovascular disease, stroke, and diabetes, all of which are factors arguing potently against using these data to guide care of critically ill children. Furthermore, in the largest recent survey of the literature, a 2019 Cochrane Review included 61 RCTs involving 12,192 patients only 533 of which were children, exemplifying the need for more data in pediatric critical ill ness [35].

For critically ill adults, several small stud ies and meta-analyses have suggested a benefit to treatment of CIRCI. A large prospective, randomized, controlled trial (RCT) demon strated decreased mortality in adult patients with severe septic shock and CIRCI who were treated with hydrocortisone early in their clin ical course [36]. On the other hand, a larger RCT demonstrated no significant benefit of hydrocortisone in adult septic shock, even in patients with CIRCI [37]. ### 41.3 Thyroid Axis

Assessing thyroid function in critically ill patients, as in healthy patients, can be extremely challenging. Ultimately, the clini cian would like to quantify the systemic actions of circulating thyroid hormones and then determine whether that level of activity is appropriate to the clinical scenario. As there is currently no direct measure of peripheral thy roid hormone functional activity, we generally depend on the patient’s serum thyroidstimulating hormone (TSH) concentration to provide an index of whether the brain is “sat isfied” with available concentrations of thy roxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). In the critically ill patient, however, this approach is no longer reliable, as the TSH level may remain normal despite a low serum level of T3, and possibly of T4 as well. This constella tion of thyroid function tests has been vari ously termed the “sick euthyroid syndrome,” “low T3 syndrome,” and hypothyroxinemia of “non-thyroidal illness” (NTI).

As type I and II deiodinases are suppressed in the acute phase of illness, excess T4 is converted by type III deiodinase into biologically inactive reverse T3 (rT3), and cir culating T3 is likewise degraded to inert T2. Recent evidence also suggests that type III deiodinase itself is upregulated during critical illness, which may further decrease T3 and increase rT3 [57]. Thyroid axis dysfunction in preterm neo nates is a distinct entity. Transient hypothy roxinemia of prematurity (THOP) has been observed in up to 50% of preterm and low birth weight (LBW) infants, with increased risk as gestational week decreases [66, 67]. Whereas the term “infants” have a character istic rise in thyroid hormone levels in the first week of life, some premature infants experi ence a transient period of low free T4, attenu ated T3 increase, and low or normal TSH levels that can persist through the first 6 weeks postnatally [2, 68]. The etiology of THOP is likely multifac torial, including early withdrawal from the maternal supply of thyroid hormone, an immature hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis, altered peripheral thyroid hor mone metabolism, increased thyroid hor mone demand, altered iodine intake and metabolism, and/or HPT axis-altering medi cations. Preterm infants are at increased risk of iodine deficiency due to loss of maternal supply of iodine and low amounts of iodine in preterm formulas and parenteral nutrition. Iodine deficiency can contribute to slow infant recovery from THOP [70]. Another contributory factor is that these infants are often critically ill, thus for a subset of infants with THOP, non-thyroidal illness is likely contributing to the pattern of abnormal TFTs observed [2, 66, 67]. Non-thyroidal illness may present differently in infants, specifically, while low total T3 is observed frequently, the concomitant rise in reverse T3 is not consis tently observed [69].

Many of those commonly used in the ICU setting have profound effects on vari ous aspects of the HPT axis and are listed below. The impact of exogenous iodine can be especially detrimental in infants and patients with underlying thyroid dysfunction. In gen eral, iodine overload from excess exogenous iodine may lead to overproduction of thyroid hormone if left unchecked. The defense mech anism against this phenomenon is a downreg ulation of thyroid iodine update and incorporation into thyroid hormone, called the Wolff-Chaikoff effect. Infants, especially premature infants, are at increased risk of thy roid dysfunction in the setting of iodine expo sure. Premature infants have greater transdermal update of iodine due to increased skin permeability, and reduced renal clear ance of iodine. Iodine exposure is possible from multiple sources, including use of iodin ated disinfectants in the mother prenatally or during breastfeeding, or directly applied to the infant postnatally; iodinated contrast media; or iodine-containing medications.

Furthermore, immature thyroid gland func tion delays or prevents the reversal of the Wolff-Chaikoff effect after exogenous iodine exposure [69]. Multiple subsets of vulnerable patients are thought to be at risk to fail to adapt to the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, including neonates, patients with autoimmune thyroid disease or thyroiditis, history of thyroid sur gery, or use of certain medications including antithyroid drugs and lithium [80].

Iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (the Jod- Basedow phenomenon) can also occur with prolonged iodine exposure and may be tran sient or permanent, with risk factors including non-toxic or diffuse, nodular goiter or latent Graves’ disease [80]. ### 41.3.2 Treatment

### 41.3.2.1 Nonthyroidal Illness

Direct supplementation with thyroid hor mone in the setting of NTI currently does not appear beneficial in non-cardiac adult patients, as demonstrated in prior RCTs [81, 82]. Studies of administration of T3 and/or T4 to critically ill adults inconsistently improved postoperative cardiac function in cardiac surgery patients, but otherwise has not been found to improve outcomes in differ ent ICU populations, and has been noted to suppress TSH which may delay HPT axis recovery [59]. It cannot, therefore, be recom mended as standard therapy for NTI in chil dren with non-cardiac critical illness. However, therapy may be justified if T3 is extremely low

### 41.3.2.2 Postoperative Cardiac

### Patients

T3 has inotropic and chronotropic effects on the myocardium that may be beneficial, as demonstrated by clinical data obtained from T3 infusions in brain-dead organ donors [83]. This data has prompted several RCTs in post operative cardiac patients. In two adult trials, no benefit was demonstrated with an intrave nous loading dose of T3 followed by a T3 infusion [84, 85]. RCTs of T3 treatment in infants after cardiac surgery have shown mod est benefits including decreased time to nega tive fluid balance and reduced need for postoperative intensive care, but data on a direct improvement in cardiac function are conflicting [86–88]. The largest RCT to date in this population demonstrated no improve ment in time to extubation or cardiac function in patients treated with T3 postoperatively, although a benefit was seen in the youngest patients (<5 months) [89]. In a prospective study of Indonesian children age 3 years and younger undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass, oral T3 was given for 2.5 days post-operatively showed a reduced time to extubation, with the strongest degree of NTI and strongest effect of treatment noted in patients 5 months and younger, though there was no difference in the ICU or hospital length of stay, hemodynamic outcomes, or adverse events [90]. Thus, T3 treatment in children after cardiac surgery appears to have little risk and may have mod est benefits in very young infants. More pro spective data are needed before definitive recommendations may be made.

### 41.4 Growth Hormone Axis

The response of the GH axis to stress also fol lows a biphasic acute and chronic response to critical illness. In the acute phase, GH increases by a factor of three to five above baseline, initially associated with a rise in IGF-I. After several days of critical illness, baseline GH continues to be elevated, with pulsatile secretion at a frequency similar to that of healthy controls, but with a lower pulse amplitude. During the chronic phase, the GH/ IGF-I ratio may be elevated well above nor mal, consistent with what has been described as a state of GH insensitivity [97]. However, despite elevated baseline levels of GH, the integrated production of GH over time is decreased during chronic illness. In addition, IGF-I is known to be much more responsive to pulsatile GH production, which is altered in this state [98]. Furthermore, during the

### 41

chronic phase (but not the acute phase), nor mal GH pulsatility and concentrations of IGF-I can be restored by continuous infusion of GH secretagogues [99]. These data suggest that the alterations in the GH axis during chronic critical illness are primarily central in origin, and not due to GH insensitivity.

Other important regulators of GH secre tion in the ICU setting include thyroid hor mone, glucocorticoids, and dopamine. In the setting of true hypothyroidism or hypothyrox inemia of non-thyroidal illness, GH has markedly decreased pulsatility. This is pre dominantly a pituitary effect, as thyroid hor mones are needed for GH gene transcription, translation, and secretion, although there are documented hypothalamic and peripheral effects as well [100, 101]. Glucocorticoids acutely stimulate GH secretion but beyond 12 h lead to a prolonged suppression of GH concentrations. Glucocorticoids also raise the serum concentration of IGF-I but inhibit its biological activity. Glucocorticoid deficiency, on the other hand, impairs the GH response to GHRH [102–105]. Dopamine infusions suppress GH production at the level of the pituitary, even at doses as low as 5 mcg/kg/ min. Rebound elevations in GH concentra tions occur within 20 min of discontinuation of dopamine, however, and persist for at least a day [106, 107].

The diagnosis of true GH insufficiency during critical illness is extremely difficult due to the dissociation of IGF-I levels from GH secre tion and to the lack of predictability of ran dom GH levels. Stimulation testing is often impractical, and may be uninformative, given that the individual is already stressed. Documentation of an elevated GH concentra tion, however, will reliably rule out GH insuf ficiency.

### 41.5 Gonadal Axis

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism has been demonstrated in virtually all studies of sex hormones in critically ill adults. In adults responding acutely to a variety of severe stresses (e.g., sepsis, trauma, burns, starva tion), there is an initial surge in LH, while FSH and inhibin remain in the normal range, and testosterone and estradiol rapidly decrease [109, 110]. This short-term response of decreasing secretion of anabolic androgens may be adaptive as a means of decreasing energy consumption and allowing substrates to be utilized for other functions [3]. As the patient enters the chronic phase of critical ill ness, they become hypogonadotropic, and the low sex steroid levels persist [111, 112]. This likely represents the common pattern of peripheral hormonal suppression and pitu itary activation in the acute phase of illness, followed by hypothalamic-based pituitary and peripheral suppression in the chronic phase. In a small study of critically ill men, intravenous pulsatile infusion of GnRH only partially overcame their hypogonadotropic hypogonadism pointing toward the interac tions between the multiple endocrinologic axes disturbed during critical illness and their interdependence on one another [113].

Recent studies of adults with COVID-19 have demonstrated an inverse correlation between total testosterone levels and both clinical and biochemical markers of illness severity [114–116]. Lower total testosterone

was an independent risk factor for in-hospital mortality. Furthermore, higher estradiol to testosterone ratios were also associated with disease severity and mortality risk, which may be attributable to upregulation of aromatase activity in adipose tissue in critical illness [114–116]. One study of males critically ill with COVID-19 found significantly higher estradiol levels and lower testosterone levels than multiple age-matched control cohorts, including COVID-19 negative patients with coronary heart disease, COVID-19 negative ICU patients and healthy male blood donors [117]. Estradiol levels correlated with disease severity in males with a trend toward signifi cance in females, but this was not seen in other studies critical illness due to COVID-19 [117]. Therefore, testosterone levels are a demon strated biomarker of disease severity in adult males with COVID-19, while an association between sex hormones and COVID-19 illness severity has not been demonstrated in females, and studies in pediatric patients are lacking.

In general, very little data exist for children with respect to gonadal axis changes during critical illness. In one recent prospective observational study, prepubertal children undergoing major cardiac surgery were found to have postoperative increases in several uri nary sex hormone metabolites, with the increases largest for estradiol and progester one [118]. Notably, however, these levels were 24-h collections pre- and post-surgery and therefore did not capture any changes in levels after the first 24 h postoperatively.

### 41.5.1 Diagnosis

Laboratory evaluation of hypogonadism should be approached skeptically in the set ting of critical illness. High or “inappropri ately normal” concentrations of gonadotropins may be encountered early in the clinical course and do not necessarily indi cate primary gonadal failure. Likewise, low gonadotropins are uninformative even in the acute phase, as they may be suppressed by elevated prolactin, dopamine infusion, or an early progression into the chronic phase of critical illness.

### 41.6 Vasopressin (AVP)

### and Dysnatremia

AVP release is a known response to biological stress, triggered by hypovolemia, hyperosmo lality, hypotension, pain, and nausea, among many other physiologic stimuli. Multiple nuclei in the hypothalamus make AVP, which is then either transported to the posterior pituitary via axonal transport, or, released into the pituitary portal system and carried to the corticotrophs, where AVP likely synergizes with CRH to promote ACTH secretion from the anterior pituitary. Aberrant hyper- or hyposecretion of AVP is thought to occur in the setting of critical illness not of primary neurologic etiology, though further studies are needed to understand the underlying bio logic mechanisms. Neurologic trauma, CNS infection or injury, or neurosurgery can also lead to dysfunctional AVP secretion. In vaso dilatory shock, which is a predominant shock physiology in adults but uncommon in chil dren, a biphasic AVP pattern has been pro posed, in which an initial, acute increase in AVP gives way to AVP deficiency, possibly caused by depletion of AVP stores, impaired baroreceptor reflex, downregulated AVP syn thesis and/or downregulated AVP receptors [119]. It remains unclear if this possible state of AVP deficiency contributes to the patho physiology of critical illness in pediatric cohorts. The potential pathologic role of AVP in critical illness also requires further investi gation. In adult patients, some hypothesized that AVP may directly impact myocardial

### 41

contractile function, alter vascular tone of renal microvasculature and increase energy demands on different renal cell populations, and may therefore directly contribute to the development of kidney injury and disease.

Copeptin, cleaved from the AVP precursor molecule during vasopressin synthesis, has recently emerged as a valuable biochemical proxy for AVP given the increased circulating half-life and biochemical stability of copeptin relative to AVP. In a prospective, observa tional study of critically ill adults, copeptin was associated with disease severity scores, multiple biomarkers of critical illness, and mortality [9]. Multiple studies have demon strated that copeptin is a significant predictor of mortality in adults with acute and chronic heart failure and with acute myocardial infarc tion [10], as well as a predictor of complica tions and mortality in severe acute pancreatitis [120].

Dysnatremia, encompassing hyponatre mia (serum sodium <135 mmol/L) and/or hypernatremia (serum sodium >145 mmol/L) has been associated with worse outcomes in critically ill infants and children. Generally speaking, there is a known risk of hospital acquired hyponatremia in children, which is twice as high in children with a primary car diac diagnosis [8]. Both adult and pediatric studies have shown that hyponatremia is an independent risk factor for mortality and increased duration of hospital stay [11]. In a retrospective study of children hospitalized for heart failure, hyponatremia (serum sodium

<135 mmol/L) either identified on admission or developed during hospitalization, was independently associated with increased severity of critical illness (inotropic support and/or mechanical ventilation) and adverse outcomes (heart transplant, mechanical circu latory support, or death) [8]. It is unclear if there is any direct contribution of hyponatre mia to adverse outcomes or if the hyponatremia is only a marker of illness severity.

Hypernatremia is also associated with neg ative outcomes in infants with heart disease. A retrospective study of infants (<1 year old) following cardiac surgery demonstrated dys natremia in half of subjects, presenting sooner after surgery in infants younger than 30 days old and a sooner presentation of hypernatre mia versus hyponatremia (median onset of 5.8 h vs. 43.8 h). There is a high incidence of dysnatremia in NICU populations, which may be attributed in part to sodium concentrations in IV fluids and blood products [11]. In a large, multina tional study of dysnatremia and AKI in NICU patients during postnatal days 2–7, patients without AKI were noted to have an increased risk of mortality associated with hypernatremia (fourfold increase) or mixed hyponatremia and hypernatremia (7.5-fold increase). The association between sodium levels and mortality was not observed in neonates with both AKI and dysnatremia. The diagnosis and management of hyperna tremia is discussed in another chapter. In the setting of euvolemic or hypervolemic hypona tremia, more traditional therapies include fluid restriction, oral urea, hypertonic saline, lithium, demeclocycline. Oral urea has been used in patients with chronic SIADH and has also been studied in patients with new diagno

Vaptans have emerged as a therapeutic option for euvolemic and hypervolemic hypo natremia. Vaptans are type 2 vasopressin receptor antagonists that function in the renal collecting duct to promote free water excre tion, and are available as oral (tolvaptan) and intravenous (conivaptan) formulations. Tolvaptan has been studied more extensively in adult patients with heart failure [138], cir rhosis [138], and kidney disease [10]. In a study of tolvaptan in adults primarily as out patients with congestive heart failure, cirrho sis or SIADH, tolvaptan enabled the correction of mild and marked hyponatremia with only 4 of 223 patients (1.7%) overcor recting at a rate faster than 0.5 mmol per liter per hour [138]. In two studies of neurocriti cally ill adult patients with hyponatremia, tolvaptan increased serum sodium levels in all patients, with over-correction only occurring in patients who received 15 mg instead of 7.5 mg dose and risk factors for osmotic demyelinating syndrome (ODS), or patients who received two 15 mg doses of tolvaptan within 31 h of their first dose, with no reported symptoms of ODS [139, 140]. ### 41.7 Potential for Therapeutic

### Hormonal Interventions to Treat the Protein Catabolism of Critical Illness

Critically ill infants and children are under severe catabolic stress. Protein loss is the hall mark of the metabolic stress response, and its extent is determined by the severity of illness [147, 148]. If protein loss persists, it is associ ated with increased morbidity and mortality [149]. Limiting protein degradation and maxi mizing protein accretion are of particular importance in children because of their lim ited protein reserves and their requirement for growth and development. Infants on extracor poreal life support (ECLS, also known as ECMO) are among the most profoundly ill children in pediatric critical care and quanti tatively demonstrate extremely high rates of protein loss [150]. Children who have suffered severe burns have also been studied exten sively in this regard and have been shown to remain catabolic for at least 1 year after their injury [151].

The hormonal changes detailed earlier in the chapter—in particular, suppressed GH, elevated cortisol, and insulin resistance—con tribute to the catabolism of critical illness. They induce a milieu of protein catabolism, carbohydrate intolerance, and paradoxical fat sparing. Stress hyperglycemia may also directly impair tolerance of enteral nutrition and exacerbate protein catabolism [152]. A number of anabolic hormonal therapies, including GH, IGF-I, insulin, and androgens, have been administered in the past in an effort to counteract these maladaptive changes.

GH (in the form of human pituitary extracts) was first used in an animal model of traumatic injury in 1941 to improve nitrogen retention and reduce weight loss [153]. Recombinant GH has since been investigated in a number of small clinical trials over a period of approximately 25 years. Small RCTs


## PDF page 1080 | printed page 1086

in a variety of ICU adult patients, using a variety of GH doses, documented improve ments in indices of protein turnover and clini cal outcome [154–157]. One moderate-sized pediatric study (N = 72) demonstrated decreased protein catabolism in burned chil dren treated from ICU discharge until 1 year from burn [158]. The adult studies prompted a large multicenter RCT in adults admitted to the ICU for 5–7 days. In this trial, which used a daily dose of 0.1 mg/kg, the relative risk of mortality in patients receiving GH was increased to 1.9–2.4 compared to those receiv ing placebo [108]. No clear rationale for the increased mortality has yet been demon strated, although hyperglycemia and associ ated immune compromise are suspected mediators. The FDA has since warned against the use of GH in patients with acute critical illness, and all related clinical trials outside of the burn population have effectively ceased [159].

Other attempts to augment the suppressed somatotroph axis have focused on delivering IGF-I, with or without GH. In normal adult subjects, IGF-I therapy has multiple effects that are potentially desirable in critically ill patients, including (a) increasing glucose uptake three-fold; (b) reducing hepatic glu cose output by 60–70%; (c) lowering blood glucose acutely (IV, not SQ); (d) lowering insulin, c-peptide, glucagon, free fatty acids, and ketones; and (e) decreasing proteolysis and thereby decreasing plasma amino acid concentrations [160]. These effects persist in the fed state, with glucocorticoid-induced catabolism [161], and were confirmed in a nonrandomized fashion in stable, post-burn adults [162]. Unfortunately, three RCTs failed to demonstrate a significant effect in ill post operative adult patients [163–165]. In stable postburn children, one RCT demonstrated significant effects in mitigating the extent of protein catabolism using IGF-I in combina tion with IGF-BP3 [166]. IGF-I has also been shown to be safe in a Phase I clinical trial in critically ill adults [167].

Anabolic sex steroid therapy in the criti cally ill with burns or trauma has produced several reports of positive results in adults [168–170] and one in burned children [158].

Oxandrolone, a nonaromatizable androgen, has been the therapeutic agent of choice due its decreased virilizing potency and hepato toxicity as compared to testosterone. Data from pediatric burn patients have demon strated a doubling of the fractional synthetic rate of protein and a substantial improvement in net protein balance [158]. An RCT in adult burn patients showed decreased length of stay in those treated with oxandrolone compared to placebo [171]. This finding was replicated in a large pediatric RCT that evaluated oxan drolone treatment in the acute phase of post burn care. This trial demonstrated that oxandrolone decreased length of stay, reversed loss of weight and lean body mass, and mark edly improved muscle strength several months after discharge [172]. Furthermore, a singlecenter RCT evaluated 5-year outcomes of safety and efficacy of oxandrolone use in severely burned pediatric patients and found improved long-term outcomes in height, bone mineral content, cardiac work, and muscle strength in the oxandrolone-treated group [173]. Although these data strongly support the utility of oxandrolone following burn injuries, whether it has a similar role in ame liorating the hypercatabolic state of other critical illnesses remains to be seen.

Insulin therapy has been studied in a wide variety of clinical situations in order to reduce protein breakdown and to stimulate protein synthesis and growth. In small numbers of healthy volunteers, insulin has suppressed proteolysis by 59–91%, in a dose-dependent manner [174–177]. In burned adults, protein synthesis was stimulated, and wound healing was accelerated [178–181]. Pediatric burn patients who received intensive insulin ther apy in a RCT had significant improvements in bone density, body fat, and lean body mass, as well as reduced markers of fat metabolism [182]. A study of four stable, premature neo nates demonstrated an 80% suppression of proteolysis but noted a significant rise in plasma lactate during the insulin infusion [181]. Another small (n = 12) randomized, prospective crossover trial of parenterally fed critically ill neonates on extracorporeal life support also demonstrated that insulin did indeed decrease proteolysis, but this study uti

However, in a larger RCT (n = 561) of young children age 0–36 months following cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, no degree of insulin therapy was found to miti gate skeletal muscle breakdown [184].

Aside from its potential broader role in preventing hypercatabolism, use of insulin infusions in critical care has been very actively investigated as a means of addressing the hyperglycemia that is common in critically ill patients. A great deal of evidence links uncon trolled hyperglycemia in critically ill adults and children with a variety of adverse out comes including morbidity, increased length of stay, and death [6, 13–16]. The PODIUM collaborative defines hyperglycemia in criti cally ill children as blood glucose >150 mg/dL [6]. Two large RCTs demonstrated that tight glucose control using an intravenous insulin infusion significantly reduced mortality by 29% in adult diabetics after myocardial infarc tion and by 34% in adult postoperative surgi cal ICU patients [185, 186]. Although these early findings were promising, subsequent tri als and meta-analyses of intensive glycemic control in critically ill adults have produced inconsistent results and have not shown a con vincing mortality benefit [187–192], with improbable benefit in traumatic brain injury patients [193]. Furthermore, the most recent large RCT demonstrated increased mortality in adults treated with intensive insulin man agement to near-normoglycemia, compared to those managed less aggressively [194].

Pediatric RCTs of intensive glycemic con trol in the ICU have largely found there to be no benefit to hospital mortality or rates of sepsis, with no significant difference in these outcomes found in a recent meta-analysis of six pediatric RCTs [195]. However, the trials that reported on the need for dialysis demon strated an association between intensive glyce mic control and a decrease in dialysis needs. In severely burned pediatric patients, a ran domized control trial demonstrated that intensive glycemic control improved morbid ity, including reduction in infection and sep sis, reduced postburn hepatomegaly, improved

metabolic measures, and reduced inflamma tory and acute-phase reactants [182]. In a small RCT of neonates undergoing congenital heart surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, intensive glycemic control significantly low ered hemodynamic support requirements and lactate levels, as well as markers of cardiac and systemic inflammation [196]. However, intensive glycemic control in pediatric critical illness has been uniformly associated with severe hypoglycemia [195, 197–199]. Overall, the current evidence does not support inten sive glycemic control in critically ill children, though there may be benefit in specific patient groups such as burn patients and neonates with congenital heart disease, that require fur ther investigation.

In contrast to the uncertainty regarding its possible benefits, evidence is unequivocal that intensive glycemic control carries an increased risk of hypoglycemia though the use of con tinuous glucose monitoring and advanced insulin dosing protocols can reduce, but not eliminate, this risk [200]. The PODIUM col laborative defines hypoglycemia in critically ill children as blood glucose <50 mg/dL [6]. Hypoglycemia in the intensive care setting is associated with complications of seizure, brain damage, and death in both adults and children [201, 202]. Therefore, the conflicting data from trials of intensive glycemic control may partly derive from increasing risks related to hypoglycemia in trials that treated to lower blood glucose targets. In summary, although uncontrolled hyperglycemia in critical illness is clearly associated with worse outcome, attempting to control blood glucose too tightly with insulin infusion does not defini tively improve outcomes and carries the risk of hypoglycemia. Therefore, current consen sus guidelines recommend an intermediate blood glucose target range of 140–180 mg/dL [13]. Further studies are necessary to assess the true benefits, risks, and appropriate degree of intensive glycemic control in critically ill children, and they are currently underway in the US and Europe. During the chronic phase of critical illness, the hypothalamus is sup pressed despite normal responsiveness of the remainder of the components of each hor monal axis. This is a state that, but for modern

critical care, human beings would not have survived to reach and have not evolved to endure. With this in mind, a final approach to hormonal therapies in critical illness is replacement of hypothalamic peptides by continuous (or pulsatile) infusion, which would be expected to reactivate normal pulsa tile production of pituitary hormones. The primary advantage of this approach is that it maintains negative feedback on the pituitary and should theoretically prevent overproduc tion of end hormones, each of which has its own maladaptive effects at excessive concen trations. For example, although GH itself has been deemed unsafe for use in this popula tion, infusion of GH secretagogues (e.g., GHRH, ghrelin) has been shown to normal ize GH and IGF-I concentrations in a physi ologic, pulsatile manner [203]. However, further research investigating clinical outcomes using infu sions of hypothalamic peptides is required to definitively address this issue.
